pwy_name: superpathway of sulfide oxidation (phototrophic sulfur bacteria)
summary: General Background, Inorganic reduced sulfur compounds serve as electron donors in many phototrophic and chemotrophic bacteria |CITS: [9328649]|. Sulfide oxidation plays an important role in the global sulfur cycle by reoxidizing the sulfide produced by sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic habitats., Phototrophic purple and green sulfur-oxidizing bacteria use the sulfur compounds as electron donors for reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation during photolithotrophic growth. Light energy is used to transfer electrons from the sulfur compounds to levels found in highly reducing electron carriers such as |FRAME:Ferredoxins| and |FRAME:NADP| |CITS: [2663079]|. Similarly, non-sulfur purple bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1061| and cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-54310| are also able to use sulfide as the electron source for anoxygenic photosynthesis., The purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| carries out the complete eight-electron oxidation of sulfide to sulfate. The process involves the formation of sulfur globules as obligate intermediates |CITS: [9695921]|. Since the initial sulfide oxidation system is periplasmic, the globules are deposited in the periplasm |CITS: [9560425]|. The sulfur in the globules occurs as sulfur chains |CITS: [11782519]| enclosed by a protein envelope |CITS: [7575095]| (see |FRAME: P222-PWY|). , In the process of further oxidation, the sulfur in the globules is reduced inside the bacterial cell to a thiol form, which is transported into the cytoplasm and oxidized by a cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation system. , At this point the cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation pathway is still not completely understood. In addition, there are several oxidation systems, and different organisms employ different systems to achieve this goal. , About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-1049| the initial oxidation of sulfide to sulfur is most likely performed by a periplasmic |FRAME: MONOMER-12314|, which mediates the transfer of electrons from sulfide directly into the quinone pool (this enzyme is described in the pathway |FRAME:P222-PWY|). This process generates the sulfur globules mentioned above. The sulfur in the globules is then reduced again to either |FRAME: CPD-846| or perthiols, which enter the cytoplasm, where they are oxidized to sulfite by the |FRAME:CPLX-7133| |CITS: [9695921]|. While the exact details of the process are still unknown, some of the key players have been identified., According to the latest model, the protein that donates the sulfur substrate to the |FRAME:CPLX-7133| is |FRAME: CPLX-8190 "DsrC protein"|. DsrC carries a sulfur atom on a cystein residue in the form of a perthiol. The source of the sulfur atom is still not clear, but may be DsrL |CITS: [18656485]| or the |FRAME:CPLX-8192 "DsrEFH complex| |CITS: [18952098]|. As the sulfur is transferred to the dissimilatory sulfite reductase an intramolecular disulfide is formed in DsrC, which is subsequently restored to its active form by the |FRAME: MONOMER-16043| subunit of the |FRAME: CPLX-8189| |CITS: [20952577]|., The |FRAME:CPLX-7133| is the enzyme that is responsible for sulfite reduction in sulfate reducing bacteria (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|). However, in sulfur-oxidizing bacteria the enzyme works in the reverse direction |CITS: [18826437]|. Reversed activity of sulfite reductase was first suggested by Peck et al in 1974 |CITS: [4526215]|, and, was investigated in |FRAME: TAX-1049| by Schedel et al, who concluded that the physiological role of the enzyme in this organism is "at all probablity the oxidation of sulfide and/or elemental sulfur to sulfite" |CITS: [Schedel79]|., A later study showed that a sulfite-reductase-defective |FRAME: TAX-1049| mutant, while able to oxidize sulfide to sulfur with specific rates comparable to those of the wild-type, was unable to oxidize the intracellularly stored sulfur, confirming a role of the enzyme in the later stages of the process |CITS: [9695921]|., The sulfite that is formed by |FRAME:CPLX-7133| can be oxidized to sulfate in several routes. The main system in |FRAME: TAX-1049| is the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8835| (see |FRAME: PWY-7457|). An alternative route, which appears to be less important, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8193| and |FRAME: CPLX-8194| |CITS:[trueper82][9004500][11685375]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The presence of the O7 antigen in |FRAME: TAX-1392869| strains contributes to the overall virulence of this pathogen, commonly found in extraintestinal infections in humans, and particularly in neonatal meningitis and urinary tract infections., The O7 antigen subunit of |FRAME: TAX-1072458| contains five sugars, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: MANNOSE|, |FRAME: CPD-14794| and |FRAME: L-rhamnose|., Like several other modified sugar nucleotide biosynthetic pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-6942| for an example), the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-14794| starts with |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is activated by |FRAME: TTP| and converted to |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps. These steps are also involved in the synthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| (see |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|) and many other deoxysugars. However, the last two steps of this pathway are catalyzed by unique enzymes - a transaminase (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.33 "EC 2.6.1.33"|) and an acetylase (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.209 "EC 2.3.1.209"|)., The region of the |FRAME: TAX-1072458| chromosome encoding for synthesis of the antigen has been sequenced, and the two functions were assigned to the |FRAME: G-17643| and |FRAME: G-17644| genes, respectively, based on their sequence |CITS: [10517601]|. In a subsequent study both genes were cloned, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| and purified, and their function was verified |CITS: [17905981]|.

pwy_name: urea cycle // Krebs ornithine cycle // Krebs-Henseleit cycle
summary: Most organisms have to deal with the excretion of nitrogen waste originating from protein and amino acid catabolism. In aquatic organisms the most common form of nitrogen waste is ammonia (ammonotelism), while land-dwelling organisms developed ways to convert the toxic ammonia to either |FRAME: UREA| (ureotelism) or |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"| (uricotelism). Generally, birds and saurian reptiles excrete |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"|, while the remaining species, including mammals, excrete |FRAME: UREA| |CITS:[13672961][13672962]|. Remarkably, tadpoles excrete ammonia, and shift to urea production during metamorphosis |CITS:[13672962]|., The |FRAME: UREA| is formed in the livers of mammals in a cyclic pathway which was initially named the Krebs-Henseleit cycle after its discoverers, and later became known simply as the urea cycle. This cycle was partially deduced by Krebs and Henseleit in 1932 |CITS: [Krebs32]| and was clarified in the 1940s as the roles of |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE| as intermediates were understood |CITS:[3545062]|., In this cycle, amino groups donated by |FRAME:AMMONIA| and |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| are converted to |FRAME:UREA|, while |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, |FRAME:L-CITRULLINE|, |FRAME:L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE|, and |FRAME:ARG| act as intermediates., Despite the generalization above, the pathway has been documented not only in mammals and amphibians, but in many other organisms as well, including birds |CITS:[4217066]|, invertebrates |CITS:[14465664][5869779]|, insects |CITS: [697760][5791517]|, plants |CITS: [13741005] [13958361]|, yeast |CITS:[11946245]|, fungi |CITS:[4996649]|, and even microorganisms |CITS:[5593971][5709377]|.

|FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| are major components of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage) in animals., They are both |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| polymers composed of repeating disaccharide units,  each containing |FRAME: CPD-12557|  linked by a (1,3) or (1,4) linkage to a uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-12521| or |FRAME: CPD-12515|, with extensive N and O-sulfation. Sulfation occurs to various degrees at position 2 of uronic acid and at positions 4 or 6, or both, of galactosamine. In addition, the amino group of galactosamine is acetylated, Many microorganisms have enzymes that enable them to degrade glycosaminoglycans |CITS: [7654407]|. This ability is particularly important for soil bacteria, which may depend on connective tissues in animal carcasses as a nutrient source., There are several steps in the degradation process. It starts with the cleavage of the polymer into smaller fragments, initially tetra- and hexasaccharides, but ultimately disaccharides. The process continues with the removal of the sulfate groups, and ends with the final degradation of the disaccharides into individual sugars, a step that has not been characterized yet. , The lyases that break the polymer to smaller fragments are classified based on the position of cleavage as either endo-lyases or exo-lyases. The endolytic enzyme can produce products of several sizes, although the final product tends to be disaccharides. The exo-lyases cleave dissaccharide molecules from the non-reducing end of the polymer chain |CITS: [9083041]|. Some lyases, known as chondroitinase AC, can act only on |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A| and |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C| (that contain |FRAME: CPD-12521|), some, known as chondroitinase B, can act only on |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| (that contains |FRAME: CPD-12515|), and some, known as condroitinase ABC, can act on both |CITS: [10618199][9083041]|., The lyases act by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disacchrides. , Chondroitin ABC lyases may help in the regeneration of spinal cord injuries that were thought for a long time to be incurable. Injection of chondroitinase ABC at sites of central nervous system injury, where a glial scar develops, removes the GAG components of ECM chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and attenuates the inhibitory effects to axon growth |CITS: [11948352][11948352][11948332]|., The removal of the sulfate groups is catalyzed by specialized sulfatases that can remove the sulfate groups at either the 4 or 6 positions. The sulfatases have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-585| but the genes that encode them have not been identified |CITS: [5647268]|.

Studies have shown that the capacity to use hydrocarbons as sole carbon and energy source, is very common, and not restricted to any particular group of microorganisms., Examples were found in a wide range of prokaryotic and eukaryotic genera including Gram-negative, and Gram-positive bacteria, yeasts, fungi, and even some achlorophyllous algae |CITS: [7532480]|., One of these organisms is the Gram negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-301|,  isolated from, machine shop cutting oil |CITS: [16560407]|, which can grow on intermediate chain length n-alkanes, (C<sub>6</sub> to C<sub>12</sub>). , This pathway describes the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-148| by this organism., The key enzyme in this pathway is the |FRAME: CPLX-3202|, which is encoded by the OCT plasmid, |CITS: [4515610]|. The |FRAME: CPLX-3202| system introduces molecular oxygen in the terminal carbon, atom of the hydrocarbons at the expense of NADH |CITS: [4403503]| to yield primary alcohols, |CITS: [7592483]|. It is composed of three components - a |FRAME: MONOMER-3842|, a, |FRAME: MONOMER-3844|,  and a |FRAME: MONOMER-1021|., The NADH-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-1021| transfers the electrons from NADH, via the electron, carrier |FRAME: MONOMER-3844|, to the monooxygenase, which reduces the other oxygen atom., The product of the hydroxylase system, |FRAME: OCTANOL|, is then further catabolized by an, |FRAME: MONOMER-1081|, an |FRAME: MONOMER-1082| and an |FRAME: MONOMER-1083|., The final product, |FRAME: CPD-196|, enters the β-oxidation-cycle, and can be utilized, as a carbon and energy source |CITS: [1453953][7532480]|.

This superpathway integrates the biosynthesis of the amino acids |FRAME: HOMO-SER| and |FRAME: MET| from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, and the single step conversion of |FRAME: MET| to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|. The sub-pathways used for construction of this superpathway are those used by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|., |FRAME: MET| (met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids, but is also required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines., In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., In the pathway shown here, |FRAME: MET| is synthesized using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of O-acylated homoserine with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine |CITS: [3309561]|., The methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| to |FRAME: MET| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., The O-acyl group of homoserine is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast, and most Gram-positive bacteria (see |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|) and a succinyl group (as shown here) in enteric bacteria and some other Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME:TAX-303| (|CITS: [3309561][9409150][10482527]|)., Once |FRAME: MET| is formed, a single enzyme, the ATP-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.6|, can convert it to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) |CITS: [6251075]|. SAM is the principal biological methyl donor in transmethylation reactions, and is also used as a sulfur donor in transsulfuration reactions, as an aminopropyl group donor in polyamine biosynthesis, and as a cofactor of many enzymes that use radical chemistry by generating a |FRAME: CPD-15400|.

pwy_name: superpathway of heme b biosynthesis from glycine
summary: General Background, Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins, including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. , In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in, transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as, |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in, modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|,, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., The protoheme biosynthetic pathway shown here is found in animals, fungi, apicomplexan protozoa, (such as the malaria parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [15144063]|), and members of the, α-proteobacteria. In these organisms the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway starts with glycine, and succinyl-CoA (see |FRAME:PWY-5189|)., In other bacteria (including |FRAME:TAX-562|) and archaea, tetrapyrrole biosynthesis begins with, glutamate instead of glycine (see |FRAME:PWY-5188|). Plants also biosynthesize heme via, glutamate for use in cytochromes and compounds derived from heme. Both the glycine and glutamate pathways are present in the chloroplast-containing |FRAME: TAX-3039| (reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [15576047], [12051904], [16093570]|)., Both tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathways merge at the intermediate |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE|., however, a branch point at |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| leads to biosynthesis of different, compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|),, |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|),, and heme D biosynthesis., A second branch point at |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| leads to biosynthesis of chlorophyll, in plants and bacteriochlorophyll in photosynthetic bacteria (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|)., In eukaryotes, heme biosynthesis spans the mitochondrial (or plastid) and cytosol compartments., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [12177321], [16093570]|. , About This Pathway, This MetaCyc pathway shows many enzymes and genes for heme biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-9606| and the photosynthetic purple nonsulfur α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1063|., |FRAME: TAX-1063| possesses two chromosomes and five additional replicons. Two genes encoding 5-aminolevulinate synthase, hemA and hemT, are present on chromosomes 1 and 2, respectively. Biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole cofactors heme, bacteriochlorophyll, siroheme and cobalamin in this organism is highly regulated and is dependent upon expression of these two isozymes (in |CITS: [7592416], [10491185]|). The hemA gene product is expressed under normal aerobic and photosynthetic conditions, under which the hemT gene product is not expressed. No activity could be demonstrated for the purified, recombinant hemT gene product in vitro |CITS: [10491185]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-1063|, no hemD gene encoding uroporphyrinogen III synthase has been identified. A , gene encoding coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (oxygen-dependent) has been identified as hemF and has amino acid sequence similarities to the eukaryotic enzyme. However, oxygen-independent , (anaerobic) hemN and hemZ encoded forms of the enzyme also exist in this organism, and there is , evidence that these two alleles were duplicated |CITS: [15028685]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1063| and many other , prokaryotes, no gene encoding protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (EC 1.3.3.4) has been definitively identified, , although the gene has been identified as hemG in |FRAME:TAX-562| and hemY , in |FRAME: TAX-1423|. Reviewed in |CITS: [12177321]|. , The ferrochelatase reaction involves incorporation of ferrous iron. In bacteria the mechanisms for acquisition of , ferrous and ferric iron depend upon which form is available in the environment and its abundance. The source , of ferrous iron for this reaction in bacteria may involve direct import by divalent metal ion transporters, more , complex mechanisms involving siderophores, other transport systems, and extracellular reductases |CITS: [12054438]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [12829269]|., In humans, the eight steps of the pathway are divided between the cytosol and the mitochondria, with the final product heme, being synthesized in the mitochondria. The pathway occurs in many cell types and is regulated in a tissue and cell specific manner. The first reaction of the pathway catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-342| or |FRAME: CPLX66-342| is considered the rate-limiting step |CITS: [23471474]|. Defects in any of the enzymes in humans, leads to a group of inherited disorders called porphyrias.

General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmospheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5265|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the peptidoglycan found in Gram-positive Enterococci , including |FRAME: TAX-1352| and |FRAME: TAX-1354|. The peptidoglycan of these organisms is characterized by having |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of the pentapeptide, and by including a |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| bridge in the crosslinks between glycan strands., Six cytoplasmic steps catalyze the formation of the |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| precursor. This precursor is attached to the memberane acceptor |FRAME:CPD-9646|, generating |FRAME: NAcMur-Peptide-Peptidoglycan|, also known as lipid I., Another transferase adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding lipid II, which carries the full monomer unit, |FRAME:NAcMur-Peptide-NAcGlc-Undecaprenols |., The next step of the pathway describes the amidation of the |FRAME: D-GLT| at the second position of the pentapeptide. , In most of the organisms which have been examined, including |FRAME: TAX-1352|, the α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is present as an amide; i.e. the second amino acid in the peptide sequence is |FRAME: CPD-12296| |CITS: [5219821][6025572][5968582]|. Some characterization of the reaction has been carried out, although the identity of the enzyme that catalyzes it in |FRAME: TAX-1352| is still unknown |CITS: [5638594]|., Following amidation, the final lipid intermediate is transferred by an as yet unknown mechanism through the membrane., The peptidoglycan monomers are polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide crosslinks |CITS: [11320055]|. While some of these enzymes are mono-functional, the main enzymes are bifunctional proteins possessing both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activities |CITS: [9791115]|., Peptide cross-links form between different parts of the peptides depending on the organism. In |FRAME: TAX-1352| the crosslinks includes an interpeptide bridge of a single |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| residue (see |FRAME: PWY-6461|). |FRAME: CPD-302| is added to lipid II by a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15487| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-11868| gene) |CITS: [16510449]| and is subsequently amidated to |FRAME: CPD-3633| by the |FRAME: G-11898|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15525|. The crosslinks are formed between the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide and the amino group of the |FRAME: CPD-3633| of a peptide in a second glycan chain., The crosslinking reaction is catalyzed by D-D transpeptidases, a group of enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin-binding proteins"| (PBPs), and involves the cleavage of the D-alanyl-D-alanine bond of the pentapeptides, which provides the energy to drive the reaction. As a result, the peptides in the peptidoglycan polymers are one amino acid shorter than the peptides in the monomers. These crosslinking enzymes are the target of β-lactam antibiotics., Penicillin Resistance, Some Enterococci, including |FRAME: TAX-1352|, are intrinsically resistant to moderate levels of |FRAME: CPD-9195|, with MICs typically ranging from 1 to 16 μg/ml., Studies performed with |FRAME: TAX-1354| showed that one such enzyme in particular, |FRAME: MONOMER-15537|, is responsible for the resistance in this strain. This enzyme, which has a a low-affinity towards penicillin, can substitute the functions of the other PBPs which become inactive in the presence of the antibiotic., While the |FRAME: G-11910| gene is located on a plasmid in |FRAME: TAX-1354|, it is chromosomally located in |FRAME: TAX-1352|, and is considered to be intrinsic to the species, although it can be treansferred among strains by chromosome-to-chromosome transfer |CITS: [16304165]|., Recently, an increase in ampicillin resistance has been observed in clinical |FRAME: TAX-1352| isolates. , Studies showed that increased resistance results from two mechanisms - over-production of |FRAME: MONOMER-15537| (expression of the enzyme is controlled by a regulator that is encoded upstream by the psr gene), and mutation of the enzyme to become less sensitive to the antibiotics |CITS: [7811006][9158761][8759860]|., A 2001 study reported that |FRAME: G-11910| is responsible for intrinsic resistance only to moderate levels of ampicillin, and by itself cannot confer high-level resistance |CITS: [11502534]|. However, this conclusion has been disputed |CITS: [18676222]|.

pwy_name: poly(glycerol phosphate) wall teichoic acid biosynthesis // major teichoic acid biosynthesis // glycerol teichoic acid biosynthesis
summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., The best characterized wall teichoic acids are those from |FRAME: TAX-224308| and |FRAME: TAX-655816|, in which the polymeric units are |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY "glycerol phosphate"| and |FRAME: PWY-7815 "ribitol phosphate"|, respectively |CITS: [13684313]|. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 1-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. The anomeric phosphate of the linkage unit is covalently attached to peptidoglycan (PG) via a phosphodiester bond to the C6 hydroxyl of N-acetylmuramate., It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: PWY-7819 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]|. , Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, The main form of wall teichoic acid in |FRAME: TAX-224308 "Bacillus subtilis 168"| (also known as the major teichoic acid of this strain) is a poly-glycerol phosphate polymer. This polymer is composed of about 40 repeating units, and is linked to the peptidoglycan moiety by a linkage unit consisting of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate-N-acetylmannosamine and one to three glycerol phosphate residues |CITS: [2692601]| (the convention used to be that three glycerol phosphate units are present |CITS: [416968]|, but more recent research indicates that it may be only a single unit |CITS: [11882717]|.), , The biosynthetic process can be divided into the following main steps: first, the linkage unit is synthesized, attached to a lipid carrier. Next, the polymeric chain is added, one unit at a time, and is glucosylated. The compound is then transported through the membrane to the outer cell wall, where the glycerol phosphate units are decorated with |FRAME: D-ALANINE|. Finally, the mature molecule is transferred from its lipid carrier to peptidoglycan. A more detailed description follows:, The first step is the attachment of an N-acetyl-glocasamine molecule to the lipid carrier |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P|, by the action of the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35530-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35530|, gene |CITS: [12101296]|. The N-acetyl-glucosamine has to be activated, in the form of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (for more information on the acivation of this donor molecule see the pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|)., Next, an activated |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| unit is added by the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35750-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35750| gene, to generate an N-acetyl-mannosaminyl-β-(1->4)-N-acetyl-glucosamine disaccharide, attached to the lipid., UDP-N-acetyl-mannosamine is synthesized from UDP-N-acetyl-glocasamine by |FRAME: BSU35660-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35660| gene |CITS: [1906927][12107153]|. The last step in the synthesis of the linkage unit is the addition of one glycerol phosphate unit, which is performed by a dedicated |FRAME: BSU35760-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35760|. The glycerol-phosphate unit has to be activated as well, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-606|, which is generated from glycerol-3-phosphate by |FRAME: CPLX-5322|, the product of the |FRAME: BSU35740| gene., Once the linkage unit is ready, |FRAME: BSU35720-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35720|, adds additional glycerol phosphate units successively, until the chain has achieved its final length. A |FRAME: BSU35730-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35730|, adds glucose molecules to the chain, usually attached to the C-2 hydroxyl groups of the glycerol. The glucosylated polymer is then exported (flipped) to the external side of the cytoplasmic membrane by the teichoic acid ABC transporter, which is encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35710| and |FRAME: BSU35700| genes). D-alanine is then added to some of the glycerol units by a machinery encoded by the dlt operon. Finally, the complete teichoic acid is hooked through its linkage unit on the C-6 of a MurNAc residue of a growing peptidoglycan chain in a transfer reaction catalyzed by any of three members of the LCP (LytR-CpsA-Psr) protein family (|FRAME: BSU35840|, |FRAME: BSU35650|, and |FRAME: BSU35520|), releasing the undecaprenyl anchor |CITS:[21964069]|., Most of the enzymes involved in teichoic acid biosynthesis are encoded by the tag genes which are clustered on a 50 kb region of the chromosome |CITS: [1906926]|. The absence of teichoic acid is not lethal for |FRAME: TAX-224308|, and mutations in the |FRAME: BSU35750| or |FRAME: BSU35530| genes, which encode early enzymes in the pathway, result in a morphological change of the cell from rod shape to a sphere shape. However, mutations in late enzymes in the pathway are lethal, due to the accumulation of toxic intermediates.

pwy_name: superpathway of heme b biosynthesis from uroporphyrinogen-III
summary: Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. It is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles., It is biosynthesized as protoheme, but different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., This superpathway shows the two routes of synthesis found in the facultative anaerobe |FRAME:TAX-562|. Under aerobic conditions, the transition from |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN| is catalyzed by the oxygen -dependent |FRAME: COPROGENOXI-MONOMER| (EC 1.3.3.3). However, when oxygen is not available, the organism is still able to catalyze this transition, using the readical-SAM enzyme |FRAME: HEMN-MONOMER| (EC 1.3.99.22), which can catalyze the transition without the need for molecular oxygen. This enzyme, which contains an iron-sulfur cluster, is able to break SAM into |FRAME: MET| and a 5'-deoxyadenosineyl radical. This radical can attack |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| and bring about the conversion to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN|., This enzyme is found in many bacteria, but does not appear to be present in archaea or eukarya (the only reference for the enzyme in a eukaryote is in the organism |FRAME: TAX-5911|, but this finding is based on sequence analysis alone, and has not been verified biochemically)., Important branch points within this pathway lead to biosynthesis of other important compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|), |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|), heme D biosynthesis, and bacteriochlorophyll (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|).

pwy_name: L-methionine biosynthesis I // L-methionine biosynthesis from L-homoserine // L-methionine biosynthesis by transsulfuration
summary: General Background, |FRAME: MET| (Met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in protein biosynthesis, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines. In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., Some bacteria can synthesize methionine using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE| with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine (this pathway) |CITS: [3309561]|. Plants use a modification of this pathway, where |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, instead of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting homoserine to cystathionine (see |FRAME: PWY-702|)., Other bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi, can use a different route in which they directly assimilate inorganic sulfur by a sulfhydrylation (see |FRAME:HSERMETANA-PWY|). In that route |FRAME: HS|, the final product of microbial sulfate reduction (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) reacts with O-acetylated homoserine, with replacement of the acetyl group by sulfide to form |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is once again methylated to methionine (see |FRAME: PWY-5344|)., Most methanogenic archaea utilize yet a different pathway. While these organisms also use |FRAME: HS| as the sulfur source, the other precursor for |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| production is |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, produced from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7977|)., Methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., About This Pathway, While many organisms seem to contain both routes for methionine biosynthesis, in |FRAME:TAX-562| and other enteric bacteria only the transsulfuration pathway is used (Greene, R.C. in |CITS: [COLISAL]| pp. 542-560). Published evidence for these pathways includes gene identification; complementation of known mutants; analysis of mutant phenotypes; and gene cloning, expression, and enzyme activity assays., The presence of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.49| was considered indicative of the presence of a direct sulfhydrylation pathway., Note that all bacterial methionine biosynthetic pathways involve acylated homoserine. However, the O-acyl group is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast, and most Gram-positive bacteria (see |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|) but a succinyl group in enteric bacteria and some other Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-287| and |FRAME:TAX-303| (this pathway) (|CITS: [10482527][3309561][9409150]|).

General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., About This Pathway, While de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotides starts with |FRAME: UMP| (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|, some organisms utilize this salvage pathway to generate |FRAME: TTP| from |FRAME: CTP|., The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-8624| (dCMP deaminase) (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.12 "EC 3.5.4.12"|). This allosteric enzyme, which is found in Gram-positive bacteria, fungi and metazoa, catalyzes the deamination of |FRAME: DCMP| to form |FRAME: DUMP|, thus providing the nucleotide substrate for |FRAME: HS11096-MONOMER "thymidylate synthase"| (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "EC 2.1.1.45"|)., While another allosteric enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase (EC 1.17.4.1)"| (RNR), plays an essential role in the de novo biosynthesis of all four dNTPs required for DNA synthesis, dCMP deaminase is specifically involved in the production of dTTP. The enzyme is allosterically activated by dCTP and inhibited by dTTP, and is thus regulated by the ratio of dCTP to dTTP in the cell |CITS: [22927644]|. Both dCTP and dTTP appear to bind a single allosteric site located far from the active site, and Mg2+ is involved in their binding |CITS: [7138806]|., The actual reduction of a ribonucleotide to a deoxyribonucleotide (CDP to dCDP in this case) is catalyzed by the rate-limiting |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "EC 1.17.4.1, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|. This enzyme, which plays a central role in DNA replication and repair, can perform the reduction of only the diphosphate form of ribonucleosides., Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase"| (EC 2.1.1.45)., Once |FRAME: TMP| is formed, two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: HS11626-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: CPLX66-1052|.

pwy_name: superpathway of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-derived O-antigen building blocks biosynthesis
summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, A group of 6-deoxyhexoses, including |FRAME: CPD-3604|, |FRAME: CPD-15665|, |FRAME: CPD-15674|, |FRAME: CPD-13462|, |FRAME: CPD-15664|, |FRAME: CPD-15695|, |FRAME: CPD-15696|, |FRAME: CPD-15698|, |FRAME: CPD-15671|, |FRAME: CPD-15672|, |FRAME: CPD-15682| and |FRAME: CPD-15681|, are used as components for the assembly of the O-anigens of certain Gram-negative bacteria. Some of these compounds are also used by some Gram-positive bacteria for construction of their S-layer., All of these modified sugar residues are synthesized in a UDP nucleotide-activated form from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| |CITS:[14670712][19710102]|. This super-pathway brings together the different routes that lead to the synthesis of these modified sugars. Note that this is a chimeric pathway - no single organism is known to synthesize all of these compounds.

In 2002 it was discovered that some organisms do not posses the thyA gene (named TYMS in animals), and instead have an alternate, novel |FRAME: CPLX-8096| encoded by gene thyX., Both thymidylate synthases catalyze a reductive methylation involving the transfer of the methylene group of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| to the C5-position of |FRAME: DUMP| and a two electron reduction of the methylene group to a methyl group. However, the reductive mechanisms of ThyA and ThyX are distinctly different. The ThyA reductive mechanism uses folate as both a 1-carbon donor and a source of reducing equivalents, producing |FRAME: DUMP| and |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE| as products, and does not involve a flavin coenzyme or a third substrate. This NAD(P)H oxidase uses |FRAME: FAD| to mediate hydride transfer in a methylation reaction that results in |FRAME: THF| as a product, rather than the |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE| that is produced by ThyA. It should be noted that many archaea do not contain the substrate tetrahydrofolate as shown in these pathways, and utilize chemically modified tetrahydromethanopterins instead |CITS: [15046578]|., ThyX shows no sequence homology with ThyA and substantially differs from ThyA in crystal structure and reaction mechanism. General Background, Heptose sugars, mostly glycero-manno-heptoses, are found in the cell surface polymers of many bacteria., They are most common in the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of most Gram-negative bacteria |CITS:[1794130][1618845]|, but are also found in capsules |CITS: [11373120]| and O-antigens |CITS: [10512635]| of some Gram-negatives, and in the S-layer of certain Gram-positive bacteria |CITS:[8720077][10406844][12101286]|. Glycosylation of an autotransporter adhesin protein with glycero-manno-heptose residues has also been reported |CITS: [11442838]|., D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units have been found in different anomeric configurations. The core oligosaccharide of the LPS of |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-573| contain short heptan chains composed of α-configured D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units |CITS: [9346320][9507008]|, while the O-antigen of |FRAME: TAX-703| was shown to contain β-configured residues |CITS: [10712598]|., Prior to their incorporation, the heptose residues are activated by attachment to a nucleotide. Two pathways for the activation of heptose sugars have been described - |FRAME: PWY0-1241| in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and |FRAME: PWY-6478| in |FRAME: TAX-143495|., About This Pathway, The S-layer glycoprotein of the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-143495| DSM 10155 is composed of disaccharide repeating units of |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: CPD-12339| units., The genes responsible for the biosynthesis of the activated form, |FRAME: CPD-12336|, have been identified, cloned, and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified to homogeneity and characterized in vitro |CITS: [11279237]|., The process starts with |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and intermediate of the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|, which is converted to |FRAME: D-ALPHABETA-D-HEPTOSE-7-PHOSPHATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15573| (|FRAME: G-11949|). This compound is converted to |FRAME: CPD-12335| in two steps - the addition of a phosphate group at position 1, and the removal of the phosphate at position 7 (|FRAME: G-11951|, |FRAME: G-11950|, respectively). Finally, the molecule is activated by the addition of GTP, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15576| (|FRAME: G-11952|)., GTP is the only nucleotide that was able to serve as a substrate for this enzyme |CITS: [11279237]|.

Level.2: Amide, amidine, amine, and polyamine degradation
summary: General Background, Creatine is a naturally occurring amino acid that is used to store and supply energy to muscle cells in vertebrates., The name creatine is derived from the Greek kreas (flesh). , The enzyme creatine kinase adds a phosphate to creatine (see |FRAME: CREATINE-KINASE-RXN|), generating, |FRAME: CREATINE-P|. The energy stored in the creatine-phosphate bond can be reused when creatine phosphate, reacts with ADP to regenerate ATP. , In fast-twitch skeletal muscles, a large pool of creatine-phosphate is available for immediate regeneration of ATP, hydrolyzed during short periods of intense work. Because of the high cytosolic creatine kinase activity in these, muscles, the creatine kinase reaction remains in a near-equilibrium state, keeping ADP and ATP almost constant,, and buffering the cytosolic phosphorylation potential that is crucial for proper functioning of cellular ATPases, |CITS: [10893433]|. , Creatine is found in the blood, brain, and muscle of many organisms. , Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate in muscle, and is usually produced at a fairly constant rate, by the body in a nonenzymatic process. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, and is mainly filtered by the kidney and, excreted in the urine. , Both creatine and creatinine can be used by microorganisms as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [Tsuru77]|., At least three different routes by which different microbes degrade creatinine have been discovered, |CITS: [10893433]|., About This Pathway, This pathway for creatinine degradation has been demonstrated in various strains of |FRAME:TAX-507|,|FRAME:TAX-1663|,, Flavobacterium,|FRAME:TAX-1269|,|FRAME:TAX-286|, and |FRAME:TAX-41273| |CITS: [8590669][9734055][Kim86][9563845], [shimizu86]|. This pathway has been studied extensively in |FRAME: TAX-243975| and |FRAME: TAX-68999|. , The first step is the hydrolysis of creatinine back to creatine, which is performed by the enzyme creatininase, (also known as creatinine amidohydrolase). Creatine is hydrolyzed further into sarcosine, releasing urea, by, the enzyme creatinase (also known as creatine amidinohydrolase), and sarcosine is demethylated by either, sarcosine oxidase (EC 1.5.3.1) or sarcosine dehydrogenase (EC 1.5.99.1) to yield glycine and formaldehyde, |CITS: [Tsuru76]|. , A study of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-303| found that all these enzymes were inducible in the presence, of creatinine |CITS: [Tsuru76]|., Since mammals do not have a creatininase function, creatinine is absorberd in the kidneys and released into urine. , As a result, measuring the level of creatinine in the blood and urine provides an accurate measure of renal function., Assays for measuring creatinine concentration are based on biosensors containing the enzymes that, participate in this pathway, meaning that these enzymes are highly important in medical diagnostics |CITS: [10893433]|., Since industrial production is desirable, creatininase and creatinase genes have been cloned, and sequenced from various bacteria, including the creatininase gene from |FRAME:TAX-286| sp. PS-7, |CITS: [7670196]|, the creatinase genes from P. putida DSM2106 |CITS: [3221393]|, |FRAME:TAX-237| sp. U-188, |CITS: [1368564]|, Bacillus sp. B-0618 |CITS: [7474433]|, and the sarcosine oxidase gene of Bacillus, sp. B-0618 |CITS: [7474433]|. , In addition, recombinant enzymes were designed, which are produced constitutively in |FRAME:TAX-562|, |CITS: [1444379][10230521]|.

pwy_name: (5Z)-dodecenoate biosynthesis I // (5Z)-dodec-5-enoate biosynthesis I // cis-dodecenoate biosynthesis I
summary: This pathway for the anaerobic biosynthesis of the unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-17910| branches from the pathway leading to saturated fatty acids at |FRAME: Beta-hydroxydecanoyl-ACPs|. , Only bacteria can produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically, and thus the key enzymes of this pathway (particularly |FRAME: EG10273 FabA|) have been targeted for development of new antibacterial agents |CITS: [22188524][23174186]|., The pathway was originally characterized in the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|. In that organism, two dehydratases, |FRAME: EG10273 FabA| and |FRAME: EG11284 FabZ|, function for the most part interchangeably in converting |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP "(3R)-3-hydroxyacyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| of various chain lengths, saturated or unsaturated, to the corresponding |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-ACP "trans-2-enoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| forms. However, |FRAME: EG10273 FabA| alone has the unique ability of converting some of the trans form |FRAME: Trans-D2-decenoyl-ACPs "(2E)-dec-2-enoyl-[acp]"| produced to the cis form |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"|., While the trans form can be reduced and elongated leading to saturated fatty acids, the cis-form cannot be reduced. Instead it serves directly as a substrate for the condensing enzyme, |FRAME: EG10274 FabB|, producing a product that can be acted on by the regular fatty acid elongation enzymes, resulting in an unsaturated acid with a chain lengthened by two carbon atoms. As might be predicted, mutant strains unable to produce active FabA are unable to make unsaturated fatty acids, but make a normal complement of saturated fatty acids., It should be noted that only α- and γ-proteobacteria have the fabA and fabB genes. Other bacterial species that produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically possess alternative enzymes, such as |FRAME: EF_RS01435| and |FRAME: EF_RS01430| in |FRAME: TAX-1351| |CITS: [15194690]| and |FRAME: G-44020| in |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [12237320]|., Repeated cycling of these four elongation reactions eventually lead to the unsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247| that are incorporated into various lipids (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6282| and |FRAME: PWY-5973|).

pwy_name: peptidoglycan biosynthesis V (β-lactam resistance) // penicillin resistance // β-lactam resistance
summary: For description of the regular peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway in Gram-positive bacteria, please see |FRAME: PWY-5265|., Two main classes of drugs that are used to treat severe infections due to Gram-positive bacteria, the β-lactams and the glycopeptides antibiotics, are targeting this pathway. The mechanism of glycopeptides activity and resistance are described in the pathways of |FRAME: Vancomycin-Resistnace|., The β-lactams are the first and still the most frequently used class of antibacterial agents. The structure of these compounds contain a D,D linkage that is very similar to the D-Ala-D-Ala bond in the peptidoglycan pentapeptide. The D,D-transpeptidase catalytic domains of the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that are responsible for cross-linking the peptidoglycan threads (see |FRAME: MONOMER-15471| for an example) recognize this strucutre and bind the β-lactam antibiotics in an irreversible manner, resulting in inactivation of the enzymes., β-Lactam resistance in pathogenic bacteria is due to production of low-affinity PBPs (for example, methicillin resistance in |FRAME: TAX-1280| caused by the |FRAME: MONOMER-15469| protein, and ampicillin resistance in enterococci which results from the |FRAME: MONOMER-15537| protein), drug detoxification by production of β-lactamases, and decreased permeability. Recently a new mechanism for resistance has been described., In some strains, such as the case of |FRAME: TAX-1352| D344M512, resistance is a result of a complete bypass of the D,D transpeptidases by an |FRAME: MONOMER-15534 "L,D transpeptidase"| |CITS: [10748168]|., The regular cross-links in Enterococci are formed between the |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue at position 4 of one peptide and the |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| which are attached to the |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of a second peptide (see |FRAME: PWY-6461|). The D,D-transpeptidase that catalyzes this linkage requires an intact D-Ala-D-Ala bond in the first peptide. This bond is hydrolyzed, providing the energy to drive the reaction., It has been shown that in the resistant strain a VanY-type |FRAME: CPLX-8039 "carboxypeptidase"| is constitutively active |CITS: [20025663]|. This carboxypeptidase, which is resistant to glycopeptide antibiotics such as vancomycin, removes the terminal |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue from all pentapeptides, resulting in peptidoglycan precursors that exclusively include a tetrapeptide. These precursors are not a substrate for the D,D-transpeptidases, but form an excellent substrate for the |FRAME: MONOMER-15534 "L,D-transpeptidase"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11907| gene, which catalyzes the formation of cross-links between |FRAME: LYS| of the first peptide and the |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| residue of the second peptide |CITS:[16144833][16647082]|., The L,D-transpeptidase is present β-lactam-sensitive strains of |FRAME: TAX-1352|, but is usually inactive due to lack of its substrate - the tetrapeptide form of the peptidoglycan precursor, |FRAME: CPD-12258|. A mutated two-component regulatory system (DdcRS) in the resistant strains is responsible for the activation of the |FRAME: CPLX-8039|, which prepares the substrates for the transpeptidase |CITS: [20025663]|., By "by-passing" the D,D-transpeptidases the enzyme confers resistance towards most β-lactam antibiotics on the organism |CITS: [10748168]|. The enzyme was thought to be completely insensitive to β-lactam antibiotics, but recently it has been shown that it is very sensitive to |FRAME: CPD-9231|, a β-lactam of the carbapenem class |CITS: [17646161]|. The discovery indicated that the spectrum of activity of β-lactams is not restricted to transpeptidases of the DD-specificity, as previously thought.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-183 "Gallate"| and structurally related compounds are widely distributed in nature. Plant lignin and tannins are major sources of these compounds, which are degraded by soil microorganisms as part of the terrestrial carbon cycle. , Gallate is also used industrially in inks and paints, and gallate esters are used as food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical antioxidants. Gallate and its derivatives are also of interest in drug development (reviewed in |CITS: [12769668]|. , Gallate and related compounds contain a benzene nucleus and at least 2 phenolic hydroxyl groups. Under aerobic conditions the benzene ring is cleaved by varioius dioxygenases. The benzene nucleus can be cleaved by ortho or meta fission enzymes, leading to different degradation pathways. Several distinct pathways of aerobic aromatic catabolism can be initiated by these dioxygenases, and their distribution among bacteria is complex |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|. Examples of these oxidative pathways are shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|, |FRAME: METHYLGALLATE-DEGRADATION-PWY|, , |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY-2504|., An anaerobic pathway for gallate degradation is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P3-PWY|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME:CPLX-8177 "Gallate dioxygenase"| is a ring-cleavage dioxygenase found in several gallate-degrading organisms that acts specifically on |FRAME: CPD-183| to produce the keto-tautomer of 4-oxalomesaconate |CITS:[16030014][Nogales10]|. The enzyme shares a common ancestor with |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, and has a two-domain architecture that might have evolved from the fusion of the large and small subunits of the latter. In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-285|, it has been shown that |FRAME: CPLX-2701| can catalyze the same reaction, although with lower efficiency |CITS: [5048285]|., The product of the ring cleavage is the keto tautomer of 4-oxalomesaconate, |FRAME: 4-OXALOMESACONATE| |CITS: [Nogales10]|. While it can form the enol form, |FRAME: CPD-185|, spontaneously, it has been shown that in |FRAME: TAX-160488| a dedicated enzyme, |FRAME: G1G01-2697-MONOMER|, catalyzes this conversion |CITS: [Nogales10]|. , The enol form is the substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-2781| |CITS: [11092855]|, and the product of this enzyme, |FRAME: 4-OH-4-ACETYL-2-OXOGLUTARATE|, is cleaved by an aldolase to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, which enter central metabolism |CITS: [12486039]|., Fluorescent pseudomonads, such as |FRAME:TAX-303|, can also cleave gallate by the ortho cleavage enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-2721|, resulting in formation of the lactone |FRAME: CPD-184| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|).

pwy_name: palmitoleate biosynthesis I (from (5Z)-dodec-5-enoate) // palmitoleic acid biosynthesis I // palmitoleate biosynthesis (anaerobic)
summary: |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| is a common unsaturated fatty acid, found in bacteria, fungi |CITS: [8294460]|, plants |CITS: [7548115]| and animals |CITS:[14321753] [6030882]|. It is formed in different organisms by different mechanisms. Only bacteria can produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically, and thus the key enzymes of this pathway (particularly |FRAME: EG10273| which catalyzes an early step - see |FRAME: PWY0-862|) have been targeted for development of new antibacterial agents |CITS: [22188524][23174186]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: CPD-9245| is one of only two unsaturated fatty acids (along with |FRAME: CPD-9247|), which together comprise about one-half of the total fatty acid content of the organism. |FRAME: PALMITATE Palmitate|, |FRAME: CPD-9245|, and |FRAME: CPD-9247| make up the bulk of the fatty acids found in |FRAME:TAX-562| membranes |CITS: [8246839]|., |FRAME:TAX-562| has three β-ketoacyl-ACP synthases (KAS): |FRAME: FABB-CPLX|, |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| and |FRAME: CPLX0-252|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG12606| and |FRAME: EG10277|, respectively., The extension of |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs| to |FRAME: Palmitoleoyl-ACPs| is believed to be catalyzed primarily by |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG10274|). Inactivation of this enzyme leads to a lack of unsaturated fatty acids |CITS: [4901354]|. On the other hand, overexpression of KASI leads to the overproduction of |FRAME: CPD-9247| |CITS: [6337151]|., It has been shown that the basal ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids in |FRAME:TAX-562| is controlled by the level of two enzymes - |FRAME: FABA-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG10273|) and |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG10274|) |CITS: [8246839]|. The former introduces unsaturation (see |FRAME: PWY0-862|), while the other elongates the unsaturated fatty acid to the level of |FRAME: Palmitoleoyl-ACPs| (this pathway)., Additional control over this ratio is provided by temperature. The proportion of unsaturated fatty acids is known to increase in |FRAME:TAX-562| with lower growth temperature, a phenomenon found in most organisms that provides a mechanism for adjusting the lipid phase transition of the membrane phospholipids to differing temperatures., It has been shown that |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG12606|), which is responsible for the further elongation of the unsaturated fatty acids to the final level of |FRAME: CPD-9247| (see |FRAME: PWY-5973|), is more active at low temperatures (relative to the overall rate of fatty acid synthesis) than at high temperatures |CITS: [7002930]|. This relative increase results in the production of |FRAME: CPD-9247| rather than |FRAME: CPD-9245|., Because the former (but not the later) can be incorporated into both positions of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|, the synthesis of di-unsaturated phospholipids occurs and the thermotrophic phase transition of the membrane phospholipids is lowered |CITS: [6988423]|., |FRAME: CPD-9245| is also found in some plants. For the biosynthesis of this compound in plants, see |FRAME: PWY-5366|.

pwy_name: oleate biosynthesis IV (anaerobic) // cis-7-hexadecenoate biosynthesis // cis-9-octadecenoate biosynthesis // (7Z)-hexadec-7-enoate biosynthesis // (9Z)-octadec-9-enoate biosynthesis // (7Z)-hexadecenoate biosynthesis // (9Z)-octadecenoate biosynthesis
summary: The obligate anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1520|, the saprophytic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1377|, and the purple non-sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-272943| produce the unusual monounsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-17289| and |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| |CITS: [14498314][5554109][6886674][12583708][23972938][Granafei15]|. While |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| is a common fatty acid in other organisms, where it is produced by oxygen-dependent desaturase enzymes, it is unusual in bacteria., The pathway used by the bacteria to produce these fatty acids has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-1377| |CITS: [23972938]|. It is similar to the pathway used by many bacteria to produce |FRAME: CPD-17910| (see |FRAME: PWY0-862|). The key enzyme of that pathway is |FRAME: EC-5.3.3.14| (|FRAME: EG10273 FabA|), which has the unique ability of converting some of the |FRAME: Trans-D2-decenoyl-ACPs "(2E)-dec-2-enoyl-[acp]"| (an intermediate the |FRAME: PWY-5971 "palmitate biosynthesis"| pathway) to |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acp]"|, which is then elongated in the usual fatty acid elongation process to form |FRAME: Cis-Delta5-dodecenoyl-ACPs "(5Z)-dodec-5-enoyl-[acp]"|. , In the case of bacterial oleate prduction, the key step in the pathway is a similar isomerization, but of a later intermediate of the palmitate biosynthesis pathway, |FRAME: Dodec-2-enoyl-ACPs|, which contains a longer acyl chain. The enzyme catalyzing the isomerization reaction in |FRAME: TAX-1377| is a unique hydratase/isomerase, encoded by |FRAME: G-44009|, which fulfils the roles of both |FRAME: EG11284| (the hydratase involved in the fatty acid elongation process) and |FRAME: EG10273|, which is essential for production of unsaturated fatty acids |CITS: [23972938]|., The enzyme responsible for the isomerization in |FRAME: TAX-1520| is still unknown, as it has been shown that the fabZ homolog in that organism is unable to perform the isomerization reaction |CITS: [19493359]|., Another key enzyme in bacterial anaerobic unsaturated fatty acids biosynthesis is the enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of the FabA (or FabQ) product with malonyl-[acp], thus allowing the fatty acid elongation enzymes to continue the extension of the unsaturated fatty acid by two carbons. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this activity is provided by |FRAME: EG10274 FabB|. In |FRAME: TAX-1377|, which lacks FabB, this activity is carried out by a trifunctional |FRAME: G-44012 FabF| enzyme, which catalyzes the activities of the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG10277| and |FRAME: EG12606| |CITS: [23972938]|., Three rounds of the sequential action of FabF - FabG - FabQ - FabK generate |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|, as shown in this pathway. In |FRAME: TAX-1377| alone a fourth round generates |FRAME: CPD-12189| (see |FRAME: PWY-7663|).

General Background, Mycolic acids are the hallmark of the cell envelope of |FRAME: TAX-1773| and related species and genera. They comprise a homologous series of C60-C90 (2R)-alkyl-(3R)-hydroxy very long-chain fatty acids, and are found as either esters of |FRAME: Arabinogalactan| or as free lipids in the form of trehalose dimycolate (TDM). Both forms contribute to forming the two leaflets of the mycobacterial outer membrane, also called the mycomembrane, which protects the organism from antibiotics and the host's immune system |CITS: [15653820][17555433][15353567]|., There is a significant variability in the structure of mycolic acids among different species. Acids from |FRAME: TAX-1716| species contain 22-38 carbon atoms, |FRAME: TAX-697025| and |FRAME: TAX-697025| spp. contain 30-36, |FRAME: TAX-37914| spp. contain 34-38, |FRAME: TAX-1827| spp. contain 34-52 in, |FRAME: TAX-1817| spp. contain 46-60, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia| spp. contain 46-66, |FRAME: TAX-2060| spp. contain 64-78 , |FRAME: TAX-1763| spp. contain 60-90, and |FRAME: TAX-286801| spp. contain up to 100 carbon atoms |CITS: [24374164]|., The acids are formed by a Claisen-type condensation of two components - the meromycolic chain and a fatty acid., Several structural classes of mycolic acids exist. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the most apolar ones, known as α-mycolic acids, contain 74-80 carbon atoms (out of which 22-26 carbons are located in the fatty acid moiety and the rest on the mero-chain) and generally two double bonds (that can be in either cis- or trans-configuration) or two cis-cyclopropyl groups located in the meromycolic chain. The cyclopropane rings are believed to protect the organism from oxidative stress |CITS: [15653820]|. α-Mycolic acids usually comprise more than 70 percent of the total mycolic acids in the cell., Other classes are defined by additional oxygen functions located in the distal part of the meromycolic chain, and include keto-, methoxy-, wax ester-, epoxy-, and hydroxy-types. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the oxygenated mycolic acids (keto-, methoxy-, and hydroxy-types) contain ~84-88 carbon atoms, and are thus four to six carbons longer than the α-mycolic acids from the same strains., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of mycolic acids could be divided conceptually into three parts: the biosynthesis of the fatty acid moiety, the biosynthesis of the mero-acid moiety, and the condensation of both parts., Mycobacteria are quite unique in having two fatty acid synthase systems - FAS-I, a multidomain, multifunctional fatty acid synthase similar to those found in yeast and mammals, and FAS-II, a system consisting of several soluble enzymes that is similar to that found in bacteria and plants., The pathway towards mycolic acids starts with the action of the FAS-I system, which has a bimodal distribution of products - forming C14/C16 long-chain acyl-CoAs and C24/26 very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs. The C24/26 very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs are modified only by carboxylation at the C2 position, at which point they are ready for condensation with meromycolic acids to form mycolic acids. The C14/C16 products serve as starter molecules for the FAS-II system, which continues elongation to form meromycolic acids., A key enzyme is |FRAME: G185E-4666 FabH|, which acts as a link between the FAS-I and FAS-II systems, catalyzing the condensation of the FAS-I-derived C14/C16 acyl-CoAs with malonyl-[acpM]. The enzyme is most active with |FRAME: LAUROYLCOA-CPD|., During elongation by the FAS-II system, continuous introduction of 2-carbon units upstream of the the double bond at position 3 results in its "migration" farther from the carboxylate (to positions 5, 7, 9 etc). Isomerases (encoded by echA10 and echA11) act at two stages of the pathway, introducing double bonds into the compounds. One isomerase acts on |FRAME: trans-delta2-behenoyl-ACPs|, forming |FRAME: cis-delta3-behenoyl-ACPs|, and another on |FRAME: trans-D2-cis-D15-gheddoyl-ACPs|, forming |FRAME: cis-cis-D3-15-C34-2-ACPs|. The action of the second isomerase results in a branch in the pathway, where some of the acids continue with an additional double bond, while others continue without it. Both continue to be elongated by the FAS-II system. However, all of the acids that escaped isomeization at the C35 level undergo an isomerization at the level of C40., Following completion of the elongation process, the acids are modified by several additional enzymes that introduce methoxy groups and convert double bonds to cyclopropyl groups (including |FRAME: G185E-4788|, |FRAME: G185E-4787|, |FRAME: G185E-4786|, |FRAME: G185E-4785|, |FRAME: G185E-4597|, |FRAME: G185E-4635|). The final modified acids, as well as the final product of the FAS-I system, are then transferred from their [acp] and CoA carriers (respectively) to a polyketide enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-8096| gene, which catalyzes their condensation into a mycolic acid |CITS: [14695899][15042094]|., Additional enzymes catalyze the conjugation of the mycolic acids first to |FRAME: CPD1G-69| and subsequently to |FRAME: TREHALOSE-6P|. Following the removal of the phosphate, the free mycolic acid is exported to the periplasm, where it is attached to arabinogalactan in the cell wall, or to a second mycolic acid, forming a dimycolate.

Toluene is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic compounds can be degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus |FRAME:TAX-286| and closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward bioremediation of environmental pollutants by metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|)., Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various species that involve different initial monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these pathways converge in the formation of 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound is a substrate for ring cleavage enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission pathway, resulting in the formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-3-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-2-OH-PWY|). , The chromosome of |FRAME:TAX-303| F1 contains a gene cluster encoding enzymes that allow this organism to grow on toluene and related compounds as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [2670929], [1916282], [8063106]|. Other strains of P. putida may contain plasmid-encoded genes for toluene degradation (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|). The inducible toluene dioxygenase enzyme hydroxylates toluene to its dihydrodiol derivative by incorporating both atoms of an oxygen molecule into the aromatic nucleus. The dihydroxylated derivative is dehydrogenated to a catechol. Ring fission of the catechol 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) is catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase to produce cis,cis-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate. This compound is hydrolyzed to 2-oxopent-4-enoate, or its tautomeric dienol form cis-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate. This tautomerization occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|. It is not known which tautomeric form is produced by the hydrolase, and which form is used by the hydratase of P. putida F1 in this pathway. However, it has been suggested that the |FRAME:TAX-303| mt-2 hydratase, encoded by the TOL plasmid pWW0, uses the dienol form as a substrate |CITS: [2681159]|, and there is evidence that the |FRAME:TAX-562| hydratase also uses the dienol form as substrate, producing a ketonized intermediate in the reaction mechanism |CITS: [9492273]|. The products of the pathway are pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and acetaldehyde, which may be converted by acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, a central metabolite |CITS: [8063106]|.

pwy_name: superpathway of L-arginine, putrescine, and 4-aminobutanoate degradation // L-arginine utilization // ADC pathway
summary: This superpathway integrates the conversion of the amino acid |FRAME: ARG| to the polyamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, its subsequent degradation to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, and finally the conversion of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC|, which is fed into the TCA cycle., |FRAME: TAX-83333| has two forms of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.19|: a constitutive biosynthetic form, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10959| gene, and an inducible catabolic form encoded by the |FRAME:EG11501| gene. When the cells are grown in an arginine-rich medium, especially if the medium is acidic and conditions are semi-anaerobic, the catabolic arginine decarboxylase is expressed, and |FRAME: ARG| is converted to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| in two steps via |FRAME: AGMATHINE|., When |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is produced by this catabolic enzyme it can be degraded further to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| and eventually |FRAME:SUC|, which is fed into the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"| |CITS:[3157043]|., There are two routes in which |FRAME: TAX-562| can degrade |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|:, In one route, which is described in |FRAME: PUTDEG-PWY|, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is transaminated with |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to generate |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, which is then oxidized to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA). GABA can be further degraded into |FRAME: SUC| as described in |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY| pathway., In a second pathway, which is described in |FRAME: PWY0-1221|, |FRAME:PUTRESCINE | is first γ-glutamylated at the expense of an ATP molecule. The resulting |FRAME: GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-PUTRESCINE| is oxidized to |FRAME:GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-GAMMA-AMINOBUTYRALDEH|, which is then dehydrogenated into |FRAME: CPD-9000|. In the last step, the γ-glutamyl group is removed by hydrolysis, generating |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| |CITS: [15590624]|., It has been suggested that the former pathway is dedicated to the degradation of intracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, while the latter is dedicated to the degradation of extracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. However, the most significant, difference between these two pathways is the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| in the latter route. One possible explanation for this is the fact that the intermediate fromed in the former pathway, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, is unstable and tends to form the cyclic form |FRAME: CPD-6124| nonenzymatically. It is possible that the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| facilitates its catabolism by preventing this cyclization |CITS: [15590624]|., The last part of this superpathway is the degradation of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC|.
